`git rebase --onto` lets you choose two things separately: which commits to move, and where to put them. A plain `git rebase <upstream>` decides both from one argument.

## Syntax

```
git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> [<branch>]
```

It takes the commits that are in `<branch>` but not in `<upstream>` (the range `upstream..branch`) and replays them on top of `<newbase>`. If you leave out `<branch>`, it uses the current branch.

## Example: move a branch off another feature branch

You branched `feature-b` off `feature-a`, but `feature-b` doesn't need anything from `feature-a`:

```
main:       A---B
                 \
feature-a:        C---D
                       \
feature-b:              E---F
```

You want `E` and `F` to sit directly on `main`, without `C` and `D`:

```bash
git rebase --onto main feature-a feature-b
```

That means "take the commits in `feature-b` that aren't in `feature-a` (`E` and `F`), and replay them onto `main`":

```
main:       A---B
                |\
feature-a:      | C---D
                 \
feature-b:        E'---F'
```

Running `git rebase main` on `feature-b` would have brought `C` and `D` along as well, because they aren't in `main`.

## Another common use: dropping commits from the middle

If `HEAD~3` is a bad commit and you want to keep everything after it:

```bash
git rebase --onto HEAD~3 HEAD~2
```

This replays the commits after `HEAD~2` onto `HEAD~3`'s parent… more precisely, onto `HEAD~3`'s position minus the commit itself. Put simply: commits between `HEAD~3` and `HEAD~2` (just one commit, `HEAD~2`) get dropped. To drop `HEAD~2` itself, use `git rebase --onto HEAD~3 HEAD~2`. In general, `git rebase --onto X Y` removes every commit in `X..Y`.

As with any rebase, this gives the moved commits new hashes. If the branch has already been pushed, you'll need to force-push, so be careful with branches other people share.
